\chapter{Synthesis --- Reading the Window}
\label{ch:synthesis-se}
\hlchaptermodality{162}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read impersonal signs and ask my way past the words I do not have.}

Complete ES-C52-sintesis-el-letrero: read the signs, ask for an unknown word, and say what the missing person buys a notice.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — reading the window}

\label{lesson:ES-C52-sintesis-el-letrero}



\begin{quote}
Almost nobody will say \emph{se habla español} to you. It will be \textbf{written}, on a window, and you will be walking past it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Four things on four windows, in one street:

\begin{quote}
\emph{SE HABLA ESPAÑOL} \emph{SE COMPRAN LIBROS} \emph{AQUÍ SE COME BIEN} \emph{SE PROHÍBE FUMAR}
\end{quote}

Three you can read completely. The fourth has words you have never met — and you can still read its shape: something is forbidden, by nobody in particular.

That is what this rung buys. Not producing these sentences, but \textbf{reading them off the world}, and knowing the missing person is missing \textbf{on purpose}.

And for the two unknown words, you already have the tool:

\begin{quote}
\emph{¿Cómo se dice \textquotedblleft{}fumar\textquotedblright{}, por favor?}
\end{quote}

Which is itself the same construction, asked out loud.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what it means that nobody is named}]
A sentence with nobody in it is not just vague — it is \textbf{doing something with the vagueness}. \emph{Se prohíbe fumar} does not say who forbids it, and that is what gives a sign its authority: nobody is claiming anything, so there is nobody to argue with. English does the same when a report says \emph{mistakes were made}.

So when you meet a \emph{se} with no doer, ask who is being left out. Sometimes the answer is interesting.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four signs aloud as if walking past them
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿Cómo se dice, por favor?\textquotedblright{} — the way out of any of them
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does this grammar mostly live? (\textbf{Written on things.}) What does the missing person buy a sign? (\textbf{Authority} — nobody to argue with.) And what do you say when a sign has a word you do not have? (\emph{\textbf{¿Cómo se dice, por favor?}})
\end{tcolorbox}
